A goblin is an imaginary creature — meaning it does not exist in the real world — that appears in folklore, myths, fairy tales, and modern fantasy stories and games. It is a small, ugly, and typically mischievous or evil being that has been part of human storytelling for centuries, especially in European traditions.

Think of it this way: just as cultures around the world invented stories about dragons, witches, and fairies to explain the unknown or to frighten children into good behavior, they also invented goblins. The goblin was the creature you blamed when things went wrong for no apparent reason.

There is no single fixed image of a goblin — different stories and artists depict them differently — but a very common description includes:

  • Small in size, roughly child-sized or even smaller
  • Ugly and grotesque — a face that unsettles you, with a sharp nose, beady eyes, large pointed ears, and jagged teeth
  • Greenish or grayish skin (especially in modern portrayals)
  • A hunched, scrawny body, though sometimes surprisingly strong for its size
  • A generally unwashed, ragged appearance

Some older folklore depicted goblins as more spirit-like and invisible, but the visual image most people recognize today — the short, green, ugly creature — comes largely from fantasy literature, films, and video games.
What a goblin is like on the inside

The personality of a goblin is just as important as its appearance. A goblin is typically described as:

  • Mischievous: It loves to cause trouble, play pranks, disrupt, and create chaos — sometimes for no reason other than its own amusement.
  • Greedy: Goblins are very often obsessed with gold, treasure, and shiny objects. They hoard things and hate sharing.
  • Cunning but not wise: A goblin is sly, tricky, and clever in a scheming way. It knows how to get what it wants. But it lacks the deeper wisdom or nobility of greater creatures.
  • Malicious: Depending on the story, a goblin ranges from a minor nuisance to a genuinely dangerous evil being. In some tales it merely hides your keys; in others it kidnaps children or attacks travelers.
  • Cowardly in isolation, bold in groups: A lone goblin is typically not very brave. But a mob of goblins is dangerous and embolden one another.

In folklore and fantasy, goblins are associated with dark, hidden, underground, or wild places:

  • Caves and underground tunnels
  • Dark forests
  • Abandoned ruins
  • Inside the walls of houses (in older folklore, they were sometimes thought to be household spirits that had turned wicked)

They tend to avoid sunlight in many depictions — a trait they share with trolls and other creatures of darkness.

Long before fantasy novels and video games, goblins existed in the folk beliefs of ordinary people, especially in Britain, France, and Germany. In this older tradition:

  • Goblins were thought to be supernatural spirits responsible for small but infuriating misfortunes: milk going sour, animals falling sick, objects disappearing, or unexplained noises at night.
  • They were sometimes tied to a particular household or location, almost like uninvited permanent residents.
  • People would leave out small offerings of food to keep goblins from causing mischief — similar to how other cultures appeased household spirits.
  • In some traditions, goblins were seen as fallen or wicked fairies, or relatives of fairies who had a darker nature.

The key difference between a goblin and a fairy in European folklore is attitude and intent: fairies could be kind or cruel, but goblins were almost always understood to be troublesome, self-serving, or outright harmful.

Today, the word "goblin" is most commonly encountered in fantasy fiction, role-playing games, and video games. Here is how the idea has evolved:

  • In fantasy literature (like the works of J.R.R. Tolkien), goblins are a race of small, aggressive, warlike creatures, enemies of heroes, often living underground.
  • In the Harry Potter series, goblins are portrayed very differently: they are intelligent, proud, and highly skilled bankers and craftsmen who run Gringotts bank. They are greedy and suspicious, but not mindlessly evil.
  • In tabletop role-playing games like Dungeons & Dragons, goblins are among the most common low-level enemy creatures — weak individually but encountered in swarms.
  • In video games like World of Warcraft, goblins are depicted as fast-talking, explosive-loving, merchant inventors driven entirely by profit.

What all these modern versions share is the core idea: goblins are small, not entirely trustworthy, cunning, and associated with selfishness or chaos.

Since goblins belong to a whole family of imaginary beings, it helps to know how they differ from creatures they are often confused with:

  • Hobgoblin: A close relative, but generally larger and more powerful. In some folklore, a hobgoblin is actually more of a mischievous but not purely evil household spirit. Today it is sometimes used to mean a more fearsome goblin.
  • Imp: Similar in its mischievousness, but an imp is usually tied to demons and the supernatural underworld — it is often depicted as a small devil or servant of evil forces.
  • Troll: Much larger and more brutish than a goblin, and typically solitary. Trolls are associated with brute strength; goblins with cunning.
  • Gnome: Usually depicted as benevolent, hardworking underground craftsmen — almost the opposite of goblins in personality.
  • Gremlin: A more modern creature (20th century), associated specifically with sabotaging machinery and equipment. Similar mischievous energy to a goblin, but in an industrial rather than magical context.

Beyond its literal meaning, "goblin" is sometimes used in informal speech:

  • To call a mischievous child a "little goblin" is often said affectionately, as a fond description of a child who is playfully naughty or always getting into trouble.
  • The phrase "goblin mode" became widely popular around 2022 and was even chosen as Oxford's Word of the Year that year. It describes a state of behavior where a person completely abandons social norms and self-care — staying in bed, eating messily, not tidying up, doing whatever they want without caring what anyone thinks. It captures the goblin's essence of shamelessness, selfishness, and chaotic comfort-seeking, applied humorously to human behavior.

A goblin, in short, is a small, ugly, mischievous, and often greedy or malevolent imaginary creature from folklore and fantasy. It is neither a noble monster like a dragon nor a helper spirit like a fairy — it occupies a distinctive space as a creature of low cunning, petty greed, and deliberate troublemaking. Depending on context, it can be genuinely frightening, merely annoying, comically bumbling, or even surprisingly capable. The word carries strong associations with darkness, disorder, hidden places, and the unsettling feeling that something small but wicked is lurking just out of sight.
